# Discussion

The present analysis was designed to evaluate whether psychotic discourse is better understood as a continuously structured system or as a dynamically shifting field characterised by localized moments of intensified organization. The findings provide clear support for the latter interpretation. Across the corpus, the association between meta-communication and delusional ontology remained weak at a global level and showed limited temporal persistence, while a modest but significant lagged relationship suggested localized dependencies rather than sustained structural coupling. This pattern indicates that psychotic discourse, at least in this case, does not unfold as a cumulative or uniformly intensifying process but rather as a temporally heterogeneous sequence punctuated by episodic configurations of increased alignment.

From a phenomenological perspective, these results invite a reconsideration of accounts that emphasize the pervasive and enduring character of altered self-experience in schizophrenia. Within the classical phenomenological tradition, Minkowski (1927) identified a pervasive 'morbid rationalism' as a continuous structural condition organising all schizophrenic experience, while Blankenburg (1969/2001) described the loss of 'natural self-evidence' as a stable background disturbance — a permanent deficit in the common-sense presuppositions that normally enable effortless social and practical engagement. Kimura (2001) similarly characterised schizophrenic self-experience as a persistent splitting of subjectivity, in which the 'I-ness' of the self becomes chronically uncertain rather than intermittently so. Building on these foundations, Parnas and Sass (2001) formalised the ipseity-disturbance model, in which hyperreflexivity and diminished self-affection constitute a structurally continuous transformation of subjectivity — and Sass (1994b, 1994c; Sass & Byrom, 2015) extended this account to argue that patients simultaneously inhabit delusional and consensual realities as a matter of ongoing structure, not episodic fluctuation. The present findings do not contradict this framework at the descriptive level, but they suggest that its discursive manifestations may be more discontinuous than typically assumed. Rather than a stable background condition uniformly shaping discourse, hyperreflexive processes may become discursively salient only at specific moments, giving rise to transient peaks of alignment between meta-communicative framing and ontological elaboration. This does not invalidate the phenomenological model itself; rather, it suggests that, in the present operationalization and corpus, its discursive expression is episodic rather than uniformly distributed.

This interpretation resonates with phenomenological approaches that emphasize variability and situatedness in lived experience. Stanghellini (2001), for instance, describes schizophrenic experience as involving fluctuations in embodiment and self-affection, rather than a monolithic alteration. The present results extend this insight into the temporal organization of discourse, suggesting that the articulation of anomalous experience may itself be episodic, with moments of heightened structural coherence embedded within a more weakly organized narrative field.

At the same time, the findings complicate classical cognitive accounts of delusion formation. Maher (2005) proposed that delusions arise as rational explanations for anomalous experiences, implying a degree of internal coherence and sustained inferential structure. While this model captures important aspects of delusional reasoning, the weak global coupling observed here suggests that such coherence may not be consistently maintained across extended discourse. Instead, inferential integration appears to be locally achieved, emerging in short-lived configurations rather than as a stable organizing principle.

Contemporary models in computational psychiatry provide a useful framework for interpreting these dynamics. Approaches grounded in Bayesian inference have emphasized the role of aberrant priors and prediction error in shaping psychotic experience (Corlett et al., 2019), while broader frameworks highlight the need to bridge mechanistic models with clinically meaningful patterns (Huys et al., 2016). The present study contributes to this effort by operationalizing discursive features and examining their temporal organization, thereby translating qualitative constructs into empirically testable patterns. In this context, the observed episodic coupling may be understood as reflecting transient alignments between higher-order interpretive processes and anomalous experiential inputs, rather than a globally altered inferential regime.

Finally, the temporal heterogeneity identified in this study invites a reconsideration of psychotic narrative as a structured but non-uniform phenomenon. Rather than assuming a continuous transformation of meaning, psychotic discourse may be better conceptualized as a sequence of shifting regimes, in which different organizational principles become momentarily dominant. This view aligns with broader theories of narrative temporality that emphasize discontinuity and reconfiguration as fundamental features of meaning-making (Ricoeur, 1984/1985), and it suggests that the structure of psychotic discourse cannot be adequately captured by models that privilege global coherence over local dynamics.
